en: The entire manifold variety of the tree of saṃsāra has its root in ignorance;
who other than the Omniscient is able to know it, describe it, and destroy it?

Formerly, in Śrāvastī, the Victorious One, the Blessed One who perceives all things without exception, dwelt in safety within the Jeta Grove and addressed the community of monks: śrāvastyāṃ svastimān pūrvaṃ jino jetavane sthitaḥ / aśeṣadarśī bhagavān bhikṣusaṃgham abhāṣata // KAvk_75.2 //
Listen for the sake of your welfare, you whose minds are purified by the light of knowledge;
I shall explain dependent origination to you in its proper sequence.
This very latent tendency of ignorance is that which effects the binding of the root of the great mass of suffering,
the poisonous tree of saṃsāra.
But the formative forces (saṃskāra) conditioned by that [ignorance] consist of body, speech, and mind;
and consciousness arising from those formative forces consists of the six sense faculties, with the mind as the sixth.
Conditioned by that [name-and-form] is name-and-form, which is designated by the terms "perception" and "manifestation";
and from this also arises the sixfold sense-base, which has the mind as its sixth faculty as its locus.
The conjunction of the six sense bases is designated as contact (sparśa);
and that which is the experience of the six contacts is proclaimed to be feeling (vedanā).
From that passion for the defilement of sense objects, craving is born;
from that, grasping arises toward sensual pleasures and the like.
Existence (bhava), consisting of the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, arises from grasping (upādāna);
birth (jāti) arises from existence through the transition into various wombs.
The continuous succession of old age, death, sorrow, and so forth is dependent upon birth;
through the cessation of ignorance and the other [links], there follows the gradual stopping of these.
This dependent origination has many modes and its foundation is established by ignorance; it should be contemplated by you who seek peace through resting in solitary forests.
It is said that when fully understood, it gradually attains attenuation over time.
Having attained thinness, it becomes even more easily warded off.
Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, the *Pratītyasamutpādāvadāna*, in the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra.
